author: Scott Turow
introFa: کتاب «The Burden of Proof» نوشته Scott Turow یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح B2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The Burden of Proof»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: DEClSlONMAKlNG IN THE COURT OF APPEAL a stage in the decision-making process because of the different role of the appeal hearing from that of the trial and the importance of the prehearing preparation. When the jury retires its views are unknown to the court. An observer might speculate on the likely verdict but the decision cannot be predicted with certainty. In contrast. the proactive involvement of the judges at the earlier stages has allowed them to form a view and commonly to express this during the hearing. By the end of the hearing the judges will have indicated whether or not there is any chance of their being persuaded by the arguments and the decision is often relatively easy to predict. The judges regard the brevity of the deliberation as a natural result of the professional nature of the appeal process and the ‘expert’ status of the bench in contrast to the lay jury. The ability to apply this expertise when reading the papers and listening to arguments from counsel and the other judges is viewed as the key to being able to reach a decision so quickly. The contrast between the length of the deliberation process at trial and on appeal is reversed at the judgment stage. The jury’s verdict is a simple binary choice which takes seconds to deliver. The appeal judgment sets out the basis for the court’s decision and is usually a minimum of several pages long. In some cases it can take almost as long to read the judgment as it took to hear the case. The judgment contains a summary of the facts of the case, the arguments put forward on appeal, the judges’ view of those grounds and the decision. The possible outcomes are also more varied. As well as stating simply whether the conviction is quashed or upheld the court may also order a retrial or substitute a lesser offence. Although the judgment is usually quite extensive it is almost always constructed on the spot. It will be given by one of the judges who will have been selected in advance by the Criminal Appeal Office and will be taken down by the stenographer to be typed up later. This will be the final form of the judgment and only very occasionally does the court reserve judgment in order to allow time to write up the judgment before it is de1i~ered.l~ The ability to deliver unprepared judgments is again attributed by the judges to their long experience of the judicial process but another equally important explanation is the fact that most of the work has been done in advance. In order to construct the judgment spontaneously at the close of the hearing the judges must be familiar with the issues and the possible outcomes before the hearing begins. Although the exact decision or the detailed arguments put in court may not have been predictable beforehand, the judges are clearly 13 Ex tempore judgments are sent to the judge who gave them in court for correction once typed up. Any major changes would require the approval of the other judges who sat. (See R. Pattenden. op. dt. n. 2. p. 124.) DECISIONMAKING IN ME COURT OF APPEAL in a position to have prepared, at least mentally, a significant proportion of the judgment before the hearing on the basis of the information provided in the papers, their readings and discussions amongst themselves. The role of consensus amongst the judges One reason why the court can direct counsel to the issues and arguments which it wishes to review at the hearing and decide cases so quickly is because of the strong role played by judicial consensus. Since dissenting judgments are not permitted in the criminal division of the Court of Appeal it is necessary for the process to encourage conformity of 0pini0n.l~ If there is a split decision, the majority decision stands but this is in practice a very rare occurrence. Throughout the process the judges work together to reach a common view. The function of the discussions between the judges before the hearing is to give them the opportunity to express their differences of opinion and to resolve these issues at an early stage so that these differences do not occupy time at the hearing. Although the Lord Justice as the presiding judge is the most senior of the three judges he does not have a dominant role in the preparation stage beyond taking responsibility for the preparation of the difficult cases. At the hearing the sense of unity is reinforced by the fact that the presiding judge often refers to the view of the court in the first person plural, for example: ‘we are puzzled by what the judge meant’. Occasionally one judge might preface a remark with the phrase ‘speaking for myself but it would be very rare for another judge to contradict ‘the point made or opinion expressed. As the presider, the Lord Justice retains a strong control over the procedural decisions at the hearing, such as when the court shall rise, but the High Court judges are active participators in the review of the issues raised in the appeal. They frequently raise new ideas and questions and do not refer or defer to the presiding judge when discussing substantive questions of law or procedure. At the deliberation stage the view of the presider carries no more weight than the others unless he has a particular experience which the other judges might defer to. The judges’ explanation for the relative ease with which they achieve a consensus so regularly relates again to their training and experience, and the fact that as a Lord Justice: ‘you’re talking as an expert to other experts’. As experts talking together the judges emphasise consensus and minimise any difference of opinion. 14 The only exception to this is cases which solely involve questions of law where dissenting judgments are theoretically allowed (s. 59. Supreme Court Act 1981). (See also R. Pattenden, op. r cit. n. 2. pp. 122-3.) 182 THE INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MDENCE & PROOF at East Carolina University on June 6, 2016 epj.sagepub.com Downloaded from

DEClSlONMAKlNG IN M E COURT OF APF’EAL The burden of proof The description of the hearing set out above suggests that there is a strong problem-solving approach in the appeal process. Although counsel for the appellant and counsel for the Crown present their cases in a way which is consistent with the adversarial process, the central role which is played by the burden of proof at trial is not evident on appeal. A conviction secured at a trial which had not explicitly set out the burden of proof would almost inevitably be quashed on appeal. In contrast, during the appeal hearing the court does not directly address the question of the burden of proof required to secure a successful appeal. At the appeal stage there is no equivalent statement on the burden or standard of proof as is set out in the prosecution opening speech or the trial judge’s summing up. The determining principle at trial is whether or not the prosecution has discharged the burden of proof whereas on appeal the equivalent principle is whether or not the judges are satisfied that the conviction is unsafe. One explanation which has been offered for the absence of an explicit consideration of the burden of proof on appeal is that it is relevant only for those very few cases in which the court is directly considering the safety of the jury verdict, rather than those based on errors of law or proced~re.’~ This distinction is, however, difficult to maintain because in all cases the court must ask itself whether the matters raised in the grounds of appeal are sufficient for the conviction to be quashed and to do t h i s it must consider the safety of the verdict.16 The replacement of the three-pronged statutory grounds of appeal in the Criminal Appeal Act 1968l’ with the new single ground of ‘unsafe’ in the Criminal Appeal Act 1995 is a recognition of the fact that the court must ultimately address this question in all cases. Even where the appeal is based on a legal or procedural error. it must still assess the weight of all the evidence in order to decide whether or not the jury would inevitably have convicted if the error had not occurred. Therefore, whether the court is reviewing a case based on a ‘lurking doubt’, fresh evidence, a mistake in the law or a procedural error it is still relevant to consider whether 15 See R. Pattenden, op. dt. n. 2. pp. 176-8. 16 Under s. 2(1) of the Criminal Appeal Act 1968 this question was raised by use of the proviso which allowed the court to dismiss the appeal notwithstanding that the grounds were proved where it considered that no miscarriage ofjustice had occurred. The court approached this issue by considering whether, if the error had not occurred, the jury would still undoubtedly have convicted. (See K. Malleson. op. dt. n. 3. p. 13.) 17 The statutory grounds in s. 2(1) were that the conviction was unsafe or unsatisfactory; that there had been a wrong decision on a question of law or there was a procedural irregularity in the course of the trial. During the passage of the 1995 Act it was made clear that the section was intended to restate the existing approach of the court rather than create a new test. (See J. Smith The Criminal Appeal Act 1995’ 119953 Crim L R 920-8.) THE INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MDENCE & PROOF 183 at East Carolina University on June 6, 2016 epj.sagepub.com Downloaded from

DECISIONMAKING IN M E COURT OF APPEAL the burden of proving that these failings and errors (evidential, legal or procedural) rendered the conviction unsafe rests on the appellant or whether the burden of proving that it is safe rests on the Crown. On the few occasions where the burden of proof on appeal has been considered it has been argued that the appellant carries the burden to some degree. During the passage of the Criminal Appeal Act 1995 Lord Scarman argued that the burden of proof is simply reversed on appeal: The Court of Appeal - and this is perhaps not always understood - inevitably reverses the burden of proof ... In an appeal against conviction the appellant goes first and puts his case. The Crown, the prosecutor, responds. When new facts are considered by the Court the appellant has to prove his case on the new facts. He has to go first, the Crown answers. No doubt he has a reply, but he has to make the going. Where has the presumption of innocence gone? ... The accused is attempting to establish a defence whereas if he was in the court of first instance, the evidence would be led by the Crown and he would have a presumption of innocence with the burden of proof resting steadily on the Crown.’6 An alternative view is that an initial evidential burden rests on the appellant to show that the evidence is credible and might have made a difference to the verdict. If he overcomes this hurdle the burden effectively shifts to the prosecution to prove that the conviction is safe.lg This analysis seems closest to the court’s practice when hearing an appeal, not just in fresh evidence cases, but in all appeals. If counsel for the appellant has not raised a prima facie case, the judges will inform counsel for the Crown that they need not ‘trouble’ him and will give the judgment dismissing the appeal at that point, the equivalent of a directed acquittal being ordered by the trial judge after the presentation of the prosecution evidence. If the court does hear the Crown, the presiding judge may specify which arguments raised in the grounds of appeal the judges feel have merit and need to be rebutted. However, the picture is slightly more complex because, while it is true that counsel for the appellant argues his or her case first, it also sometimes occurs that the appellant is not required to present his grounds at all. In such cases the judges indicate that they are provisionally inclined to quash the 18 Hansard. HL 8/6/95 cols 1497-8. 19 See R. Pattenden op. cit. n. 2 for a fuller discussion of this issue. 184 THE INTERNAllONAL JOURNAL OF MDENCE & PROOF at East Carolina University on June 6, 2016 epj.sagepub.com Downloaded from

DEClSlONMAKlNG IN M E COURT OF APPEAL conviction unless the Crown can persuade them otherwise. It then falls on the Crown to reverse the judges’ presumption that the conviction is unsafe. In other cases, although counsel for the appellant is called upon to present the grounds, it is apparent from the nature of the judges’ questions and comments that they came into court with a provisional view in favour of the appellant’s case. This indicates that the position regarding the burden of proof is not static; that it can move from appellant to the Crown depending on the preliminary view which the judges have formed from reading the papers. In most appeals the initial burden lies with the appellant who brings the case and so must prove it by persuading the judges that the conviction is unsafe. But the position is very different when the court has taken a supportive view of the appeal from the papers and in these cases it can be argued that the burden is effectively borne by the Crown who will then, in Lord Scarman’s words ‘have to make the going’. Since the burden of proof is not an expliat feature of the appeal process it may be more appropriate to conclude that it does not play the same role on appeal as at trial. Instead, the appeal hearing is in this respect analogous with an inquisitorial hearing. During a trial in an inquisitorial system such as those operating in France, Belgium or Germany, the defendant is convicted if the judge believes him or her to be guilty. Although the presumption of innocence is present, the decision is made without reference to the burden of proof. In the Court of Appeal the judges quash the conviction if they believe it to be unsafe. The test they generally apply when reviewing legal or procedural errors is whether they believe that the jury would undoubtedly still have convicted if the error set out in the grounds of appeal had not occurred.20 This test is similarly applied without reference to the burden of proof in that the court does not speafy how certain it must be that the jury would undoubtedly still have convicted. The inquisitorial trial differs from the appeal hearing in that it is a full fact-finding forum which operates without restrictive rules of evidence, whereas the appeal hearing is a very limited review of a particular error or problem, but the approach to the burden of proof is equivalent. Conclusion I have argued that the preparation stage plays a crucial role in influencing the final decision on appeal. From reading the papers and in discussion the judges form a preliminary view which they bring to the hearing. On the basis of this view they highlight and clarify the issues which they want to address and test the arguments being put by counsel in a fast and focused 20 In ‘lurking doubt’ cases the test is a subjective one of whether the court itself feels the conviction is unsafe. (See K. Malleson op. cit. n. 3. pp. 11-12.) THE INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL of EVIDENCE & PROOF 185 at East Carolina University on June 6, 2016 epj.sagepub.com Downloaded from

DECISIONMAKING IN M E COURT OF APPEAL problem-solving process. If the burden of proof can be said to have any relevance at all on appeal. it rests on whichever party must reverse the preliminary view and the prospects for doing so are slight. The advantages of this focused problem-solving process which addresses discrete questions that are identified in advance by forming an initial view on the matter is that the court can process a heavy workload quickly. During a trial unforeseen issues frequently emerge which require attention, but on appeal the questions to be considered can be much more strictly predetermined. The grounds of appeal set out the parameters of the questions which the court is being asked to consider and the role of counsel is much more strictly circumscribed by the judges. Their preliminary view focuses on those issues which the judges are concerned to address and these are dealt with systematically during the hearing. The judges’ ability to highlight the relevant points from the papers and to reach a decision quickly is attributed by them to their experience and their status as ‘experts’. This is supported by a strong culture of consensus amongst the judges which assists them in reaching a common view in almost all cases. The result is that the Court of Appeal decides cases in hours which have occupied the trial court for days, weeks or even months. The disadvantages of this process are partly those of all inquisitorial methods of proof, that the preliminary view constructed before the hearing can be extremely difficult to overturn. A common criticism of the French system for example, is that the pretrial dossier prepared by the juge d’instruction remains the final word at trial. Similarly the dominant role played by the preliminary view formed by the appeal judges from reading the papers and in discussion before the hearing makes it very hard to reverse. The proactive approach of the judges at the hearing may inhibit counsel from setting out alternative points fully and so prevent new and important issues from being considered. 186 THE INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EVIDENCE & PROOF at East Carolina University on June 6, 2016 epj.sagepub.com Downloaded from
